'''''Callitriche stagnalis''''' is a perennial aquatic vascular plant species.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.eddmaps.org/ipane/ipanespecies/aquatics/Callitriche_stagnalis.cfm?|title=Callitriche stagnalis|website=EDDMapS.org|language=en|access-date=2019-02-12}}</ref> Also known as pond water-starwort, ''C. stagnalis,'' may thrive in a variety of aquatic and subaquatic habitats, specially those exhibiting slowly moving to non-moving water.<ref name=":0" /> Although ''C. stagnalis'' does not pose a threat to humans, its reproductive rate may pose a threat to native vegetation  in areas where it has been introduced,<ref name=":0" /> as the resulting dense vegetative mats frequently out-compete native species.<ref name=":0" />

== Morphology ==

=== General structure ===
[[File:Callitriche stagnalis leaf1 (12079443754).jpg|thumb|Leaves of ''C. stagnalis''.]]
The general appearance of ''C. stagnalis'' differs slightly depending on whether the plant being viewed was submerged or floating.<ref name=":0" /> Both exhibit long stems that vary in length from approximately 1 to 3 decimeters.<ref name=":0" /> These stems give rise to leaves that are oppositely arranged.<ref name=":0" /> The characteristic difference between the submerged and floating ''C. stagnalis'' is its leaf shape.<ref name=":0" /> Submerged leaves of ''C. stagnalis'' are linear, appearing long and thin with one vein running up the center.<ref name=":0" /> Floating leaves of ''C. stagnalis'', however, may be spatulate to obovate in shape, which appear much wider that the typical submerged leaves, and contain a much larger number of veins (5-7).<ref name=":0" /> Growth of the leaves of ''C. stagnalis'' also differs depending on whether they are submerged or floating.<ref name=":0" /> Submerged leaves can grow 4 to 10 mm in length whereas floating leaves may only reach 2 mm in length.<ref name=":0" /> Submerged leaves are typically thin but may be wider in some cases making it harder to differentiate them from their floating counterparts which may grow 5 to 8 mm in width.<ref name=":0" />

=== Reproductive structure ===
''Callitriche stagnalis'' is a monoecious plant, having both female and male reproductive structures.<ref name=":0" /> ''C. stagnalis'' staminate and pistillate flowers contain the stamen (male reproductive organ that fertilizes via pollen) and the pistil (female reproductive organ), respectively.<ref name=":0" /> Small distances between flower types of ''C. stagnalis'' promotes aerial self-pollination.<ref name=":0" /> Another structural feature that may aid pollination are the two distinct bracts located at the base of each flower.<ref name=":0" /> These small bracts aid in keeping the flowers above water.<ref name=":0" /> ''C. stagnalis'' produces fruit that is suborbicular in shape.<ref name=":0" /> This fruit varies in thickness from 1.5 to 2 mm and is composed of multiple thin, winged margin mericarps.<ref name=":0" />

== Dispersal mechanism ==
Clonal spread and prolific seed production are two strategies promoting the distribution of ''C. stagnalis.''<ref name=":0" /> Because this species is able to perform self pollination, it is able to achieve greater seed production assisting dispersal.<ref name=":0" /> Seeds may also be further spread to distant areas by vectors such as bird, boats, and tires.<ref name=":0" /> This species has also been known to spread through plant fragmentation.<ref name=":0" /> The ability of ''C. stagnalis'' to reproduce via clonal spread aids in this species invasiveness and subsequent threat to native vegetation.<ref name=":0" />

== Habitat ==
''Callitriche stagnalis'' is normally found in aquatic environments particularly in which there is little to no motion.<ref name=":0" /> ''C. stagnalis'' frequents lakes, ponds, salt marshes, and slow moving rivers and streams.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/callitriche/stagnalis/|title=Callitriche stagnalis (pond water-starwort): Go Botany|website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org|access-date=2019-02-12}}</ref> This species is able to thrive in both fresh and brackish water habitats.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

== Distribution world-wide ==
''Callitriche stagnalis'' is native to both Europe and North Africa, where it is widespread in aquatic and subaquatic habitats.<ref name=":0" />
Currently ''C. stagnalis'' has been found in Europe, Northern Africa, The United States, Asia, Australia, New Caledonia, and New Zealand.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Philbrick|first=C. Thomas|date=Winter 1998|title=INVASION AND SPREAD OF CALLITRICHE STAGNALIS (CALLITRICHACEAE) IN NORTH AMERICA|journal=Rhodora|volume=100|pages=25–38|jstor=233132667}}</ref>

=== Introduction to the United States ===
The earliest record of ''C. stagnalis'' in North America comes from New York and New Jersey in 1861.<ref name=":0" /> And, it was first found on the West Coast in 1871 in Oregon.<ref name=":0" /> Though the exact mechanism of its introduction is unclear, its existence suggests that it may have been accidentally released through shipping.<ref name=":0" /> By the end of the nineteenth century, it had become a popular aquarium plant, this is believed to be the reason why the invasion is not only focused on the coasts of the United States and has been able to enter inland states.<ref name=":0" />

''Callitriche stagnalis'' is found in all of the mid-Atlantic states (New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Delaware and West Virginia), Virginia, Tennessee, Alabama, Wisconsin, Montana, Washington, Oregon and California.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> In New England, it has been reported in Massachusetts, Connecticut and Maine.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

=== Invasive threat ===
[[File:Callitriche stagnalis Scop. (AM AK309216-1).jpg|thumb|Dense vegetative mat of ''C. stagnalis''.]]
Although this species does not pose a threat to humans, it has the potential to threaten native and other local vegetation.<ref name=":0" /> Due to this species ability to reproduce by clonal spread, ''C. stagnalis'' can form thick and locally dense vegetative mats which can crowd out other vegetation by taking up limited space and nutrients in the environment.<ref name=":0" />
